title: TTL
subtitle: Time-To-Live expiration mechanics, active vs passive expiry in Redis, and TTL jitter to prevent synchronized thundering herds.
keyTakeaways: Every cached key should have an explicit Time-To-Live (TTL) as a safety net to bound maximum staleness even if active invalidation fails.
Synchronized TTLs (e.g., setting 10,000 keys with `EX 3600` during a batch job) cause a Cache Avalanche when all keys expire at the exact same second: always add random jitter.
Caches reclaim expired keys using a combination of Passive Expiry (on read access) and Active Expiry (probabilistic background sampling).

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: If a Redis instance holds 50 million keys with TTLs, running a timer thread for every key would consume massive CPU. Instead, Redis combines two lightweight strategies: Passive Expiration and Active Probabilistic Expiration.
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: Every cached key should have an explicit Time-To-Live (TTL) as a safety net to bound maximum staleness even if active invalidation fails.

**Problem Space & Invariants**: Synchronized TTLs (e.g., setting 10,000 keys with `EX 3600` during a batch job) cause a Cache Avalanche when all keys expire at the exact same second: always add random jitter.
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: Distributed architectures apply specific implementation patterns and topologies for TTL:
bullets: **Short TTL (e.g., 5–30 seconds)**: Provides minimizes staleness window without requiring complex event-driven cache invalidation. Best suited for High-traffic endpoints where slight staleness is acceptable (e.g., trending lists, live scores).

**Long TTL + Event-Driven Invalidation + Soft TTL**: Provides maximizes cache hit ratio (>99%) and serves zero-latency reads via stale-while-revalidate. Best suited for Product catalogs, user profiles, and configuration settings.

Passive (Lazy) Expiration: When a client executes `GET key`, Redis checks if the key's expiration timestamp has passed. If expired, it deletes the key immediately and returns `nil`. Caveat: keys that are never read again would sit in RAM forever without active expiry.

Active Probabilistic Sampling: 10 times per second, Redis samples 20 random keys from the set of keys with an associated TTL. It deletes any expired keys found. If >25% of the 20 sampled keys were expired, it repeats the loop immediately.
Mandatory TTL Jitter: Always compute `ttl = base_ttl + random(0, jitter_window)` on every `SET` operation to spread expirations uniformly over time.
Tiered TTLs by Volatility: Static reference data = 24h; user profile = 1h; dynamic feed counts = 30s.

sections.heading: 3. Production Strengths: Where & How to Apply
sections.body: Production deployments apply TTL across targeted operational scenarios:
bullets: **Where to Use: High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for High-traffic endpoints where slight staleness is acceptable (e.g., trending lists, live scores), suited for environments requiring Minimizes staleness window without requiring complex event-driven cache invalidation.

**Where to Use: High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for Product catalogs, user profiles, and configuration settings, where Maximizes cache hit ratio (>99%) and serves zero-latency reads via Stale-While-Revalidate.

**How to Use: Engineering Implementation**: A Cache Avalanche occurs when a large batch of keys is populated at the same moment (for example, after a deployment, cron job, or regional failover) with an identical static TTL like `3600` seconds. Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.
**Architectural Leverage**: Provides predictable resource boundaries, bounds blast radius, and optimizes cost per transaction.

sections.heading: 4. Failure Modes & Trade-Offs: When to Avoid
sections.body: Improper implementation of TTL introduces operational bottlenecks and failure modes:
bullets: **Where to Avoid: Trade-Off Bottlenecks**: Avoid when constraints cannot tolerate: lower cache hit ratio for long-tail items; higher baseline read load on the database.
**Where to Avoid: Complexity Ceiling**: Avoid when operational requirements do not justify: requires reliable invalidation pipelines (cdc or pub/sub) to clear changed items.
**Catastrophic Failure Modes**: Uncalibrated parameters can trigger queue exhaustion, thread starvation, cascading retry storms, and tail latency amplification.
**Operational Overhead**: Requires continuous observability (p95/p99 latency tracking, saturation alerts, and distributed tracing across hop boundaries).

sections.heading: 5. Staff+ Engineering Verdict & Interview Playbook
sections.body: Technical guidelines and evaluation criteria for TTL:
bullets: **Staff+ Golden Rule**: Caches reclaim expired keys using a combination of Passive Expiry (on read access) and Active Expiry (probabilistic background sampling).
**Staff+ Interview Playbook**: Mentioning 'Soft TTL + Hard TTL (Stale-While-Revalidate)' and 'TTL Jitter to prevent Cache Avalanche' is an easy way to stand out when discussing caching layers.
